Disclosure Day: 4K Ultra HD + Blu-ray + Digital Code

Reviewed by:
Luke Bonanno on August 31, 2026

Theatrical Release:
June 12, 2026

Movie Listings & Theater Showtimes

Spielberg's latest alien adventure comes home in style.

Running Time146 min

RatingPG-13

Running Time 146 min

RatingPG-13

Steven Spielberg

David Koepp (screenplay), Steven Spielberg (story)

Disclosure Day: 4K Ultra HD + Blu-ray + Digital Code (2026)

by Luke Bonanno

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 10:21
Instaread

If people know just one thing about Steven Spielberg, it’s that he makes blockbusters. Spielberg has long been celebrated as the McDonald’s of the  movie world and he’s been around nearly as long, with his first big hit (Jaws) arriving more than half a century ago. Lately, though, Spielberg hasn’t really lived up to this reputation of mainstream appeal.

Movies

In the 21st century, Spielberg has been drawn to history, be it of American politics (like Lincoln) or his own personal upbringing (The Fabelmans). Sure, his name appears on overtly commercial fare like the Transformers and Jurassic World franchises, but only as producer. And while he still on occasion swings big for general audiences with broadly-appealing works like Ready Player One (2018), The BFG (2016), and The Adventures of Tintin (2011) and some of those have indeed generated profits, the  movies have decidedly not set the world on fire the way his past triumphs like E.T., Raiders of the Lost Ark, and Jurassic Park did in decades past.

That brings us to Disclosure Day, Spielberg’s thirty-seventh and latest film as director. It’s a big summer movie coming from one of the big studios (Universal) and carrying a relatively big budget (though far from today’s higher end efforts). It is not expected to court prestige or compete for above-the-line Academy Awards. But, nonetheless, it is still a work from one of the greatest American filmmakers of all time, an undertaking that has attracted in-demand movie actors and esteemed longtime Spielberg collaborators like composer John Williams and cinematographer Janusz Kamiński.

Disclosure Day credits its screenplay entirely to David Koepp, a veteran whose big screen adaptations include Jurassic Park, Mission: Impossible, the first Tobey Maguire Spider-Man, and Spielberg’s 2005 War of the Worlds. Perhaps more notably, the story is attributed to Spielberg, something he has rarely taken credit for since the early days in his career. The subject is extraterrestrial life, a topic Spielberg is no stranger to, having Close Encounters of the Third Kind and E.T.: The Extra-Terrestrial among the most popular and well-known of his early credits.

Science Fiction & Fantasy Films

The scientific curiosity and wide-eyed wonder of Spielberg’s early films return here to an industry where otherworldly spectacle and grand visual effects are now consistently among the biggest draws. Spielberg’s impact on mainstream cinema of the past half-century cannot be overstated, but he personally seems to have tired of crafting big, ambitious four-quadrant adventures. And yet here he is, age 79, with an estimated net worth between seven and twelve billion dollars, revealing to us that he still wonders about our place in the universe.

Disclosure Day opens at a wrestling match where thirtysomething tech wizard Daniel Kellner (Josh O’Connor) is being threatened and pursued by powerful parties who want the MacGuffins he’s been carrying around in a backpack. These are powerful MacGuffins that could shed light on buried scientific discoveries and confirm the existence of intelligent extraterrestrial life. The hunt comes to also involve Margaret Fairchild (Emily Blunt), a Kansas City meteorologist with news anchor ambitions who suddenly, inexplicably finds herself disarming others and herself with newly-unlocked ability to speak in foreign tongues and know specific things about complete strangers.

Daniel and Margaret are on the radars of a powerful corporation who has historically suppressed extraordinary findings. The corporation is led by the exacting Noah Scanlon (Colin Firth) and also employs a stealth defector Hugo Wakefield (Colman Domingo), who is pushing for disclosure.

Blu-Ray Players & Recorders

When Spielberg shot Close Encounters back in 1976, nobody was making speculative sci-fi movies like that and certainly not in a way that could be taken seriously. Nowadays, we have entire cinematic universes that are all about constructing elaborate myths and grounding them in something that resembles our reality. These are works of escapism that are more invested in managing brands and budgets and meeting shareholder expectation and moviegoer demand than in genuine galactic exploration. But people see them in great numbers, enjoying them in a way that makes them the present-day descendants of Spielberg’s yesteryear alien movies.

Movies

Disclosure Day will not be mistaken for today’s superhero fare, but, for better or worse, it still has a lot in common with them. Whereas those superhero movies strategically plot out long-term timelines, overlaps, and spin-offs, this one only concerns itself with the two and a half hours it requires of you now. Those hours are filled with another fine score from John Williams, now 94 years old, polished and appealing visuals courtesy of Kamiński, and a serviceable cast that brings respect for the director but still keeps things mostly sharp and spry.

In my theatrical review, I wrote that the  movie’s success or failure would be determined by how much it resonated with the public, both the young moviegoers Hollywood primarily targets and the more cynical, discerning adults who grew up on Spielberg’s imaginative crowd-pleasers. These days, every new release of ambition seems to be treated as some grand assessment of the status and future of the moviegoing experience. This one has the added challenge of determining whether or not Spielberg still knows how to attract big crowds. On that basis, Disclosure Day cannot easily be deemed either an outright success or a clear flop. The movie grossed $117 million domestically and $241 million worldwide. We would have to turn back the clock a few decades for those to be considered blockbuster numbers on a major studio release. The grosses are in the neighborhood of A.I. and Minority Report, but only if we ignore a quarter-century’s worth of inflation.

Music Composition & Theory

Perhaps, more significantly to those of us who don’t own Comcast stock, public sentiment towards the film is pretty mixed. A movie’s legacy is determined by more than just the initial wave of reactions. I recall The Lost World: Jurassic Park being reviled upon its release twenty-nine years ago and today it sits with a fairly respectable 6.6 user rating on IMDb and 3.2 on Letterboxd. Both of those numbers are slightly higher than what Disclosure Day has currently settled at, a 6.4 on IMDb and a 3.0 on Letterboxd.

In truth, while the divisive response is at odds with Spielberg’s heyday, it’s not off the mark, especially when you read into the substance of the disapprovals, discussing the film’s somewhat out of touch read on society. I wish I could declare Disclosure Day a rousing return to form for Spielberg, but honestly he doesn’t need a return to form given the high caliber of  movies he’s been steadily making. And I’m not sure that cinema needs him to bring back the methods with which he dominated the box office for nearly the entire 1980s. The medium must evolve and Spielberg, impressively, still is. We’re all better off that he is continuing to explore new worlds and contribute to the medium in grand fashion.

Blu-Ray Players & Recorders

While Spielberg movies used to sell tickets all summer long, theatrical release windows have gotten much shorter, so it’s not much of a surprise that Disclosure Day has hit physical media by the end of the summer. Last week, Universal put out the film on  DVD, Blu-ray, and the 4K Ultra HD + Blu-ray + Digital Code combo pack reviewed here.

VIDEO and AUDIO

Even the Spielberg films that don’t bowl you over dramatically tend to be difficult to criticize on a technical level and, although some have griped about its CGI animals, Disclosure Day still provides a dynamic cinematic experience, which of course gets translated to 4K and Blu-ray without any concerns. This likely won’t win technical Oscars, but it could definitely draw some nominations and even if it doesn’t, it’ll give your home theater an agreeable workout.

Science Fiction & Fantasy Films

BONUS FEATURES, MENUS, PACKAGING and DESIGN

Though it is labeled a Collector’s Edition, Disclosure Day is joined only by two bonus features here. Gladly, one of the two is substantial, narrowly meeting the Academy’s definition of feature length.

“Entering the Unknown: Inside Disclosure Day” (54:03) is a thorough making-of documentary which hails from longtime Spielberg documentarian Laurent Bouzereau. It sheds much light on both the “how” and “why” this movie was made, which would give detractors some insight in the unlikely event they find themselves with access to this and willing to set aside an hour to watch it. Though fairly slick and routine, Spielberg fans will find this companion to the feature easy to appreciate, despite the abundance of distractingly blurred clothing logos.

“Spielberg & Williams: A Legendary Collaboration” (4:09) celebrates the director and composer as they team up for their thirtieth film together. It’s pretty wild seeing Williams still working in his mid-90s, but given its brevity, this piece doesn’t go into the detail you might like. For that, you’ll have to turn to one of the multiple good feature-length documentaries on Williams. Here, we pretty much just get to see Williams addressing his orchestra and a little crew celebration of the duo with a lavish chocolate cake.

No trailers for Disclosure Day or anything else are included here. An insert supplies a digital copy code and accompanies the two discs inside the slipcovered black keepcase.

Movies

Silent video previews of the two bonus features play in a pop-up over the static, scored, minimalist menu.

CLOSING THOUGHTS

Steven Spielberg’s grip on the moviegoing public may be loosening, but Disclosure Day demonstrates that he still is capable of delivering high quality, fantastical thrills. This almost certainly won’t be your favorite Spielberg  movie or one of your absolute favorites of 2026, but it’s a well-made popcorn flick that holds your interest and makes you think. For Spielberg to still be making big movies like this on the cusp of 80 is a huge deal that any fan of cinema and pop culture would be foolish to take for granted.

Universal’s 4K combo pack delivers a super high quality presentation in three formats and a substantial hour-long making-of documentary as well.
